headline_en: Labour market dependent on the Middle East; uncertainty because of the war
summary_en: After the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February 2026 and the war spread across the Middle East, flights from Dhaka became irregular, BMET clearances for the first 10 days of March 2026 fell by about half compared with a year earlier, and workers home on leave from Oman were stuck. The article gives BMET figures on how concentrated Bangladesh's overseas employment is (67% to Saudi Arabia in 2025), lists closed markets (Malaysia, Oman, Bahrain, UAE), and reports ministry steps: a hotline and control room, a request to extend visas, and Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and UAE extending visa validity to 31 March. RMMRU warns of irregular migration and of a ring sending Bangladeshis recruited for Russia into the Russia-Ukraine war.

facts.statement: BMET data: in the first 10 days of March 2026, clearances (smart card/exit clearance) taken to go abroad for work fell by about 50 percent compared with the same period of the previous year: 21,122 people took clearance on 1-10 March 2026 against 46,744 in the same period of 2025.
BMET says 65,613 workers went abroad to various countries in February 2026, of whom about 38,000 went in the first 10 days of the month.

BMET data: although 168 countries are on the list of destinations for sending workers, in 2025 Bangladeshi workers went to 141 countries; 90 percent went to only 5 countries, 13 countries received just 1 worker each and 34 countries received 2 to 10 workers each.
In 2025 a total of 1,130,757 Bangladeshi workers went abroad, and 67 percent of them went to Saudi Arabia.

Malaysia's labour market has been closed to Bangladeshi workers since June 2024 over allegations of a syndicate (chokro) doing business in recruitment; the interim government took initiatives but could not reopen it, and as of March 2026 it had been closed for about two years.
During 2025 it was not possible to reopen several closed labour markets including Oman and Bahrain, and as of March 2026 the United Arab Emirates market had still not properly opened.

During the interim government's time Bangladesh signed a total of seven agreements with Italy, South Korea, Japan and Saudi Arabia to expand the labour market; the article says skilled workers can be sent if these are put to use.
Officials and recruiters say Bangladesh cannot send workers to promising markets such as Europe and Japan because it has not been able to produce skilled workers.
facts.source_in_article: officials and businesspeople involved in sending workers

facts.statement: In the ongoing war (which began 28 February 2026), two expatriate Bangladeshis had died in Saudi Arabia, one in Bahrain and one in the United Arab Emirates as of the article's date.

The body of the Bangladeshi expatriate killed in the UAE in the war has been buried (in the UAE), and the process of bringing back the bodies of the others (killed in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain) is under way, according to the expatriates' welfare ministry.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment sources

facts.statement: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment has opened a round-the-clock hotline and control room to help expatriates affected by the Middle East war (the article prints no number).
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment sources

facts.statement: On 9 March 2026 the expatriates' welfare ministry asked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to get visa validity extended for affected and stranded workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment sources

facts.statement: Following requests through Bangladesh's embassies, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates decided to extend visa validity until 31 March (2026) for those who could not travel because of the war.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Nurul Haque Nur

facts.statement: State Minister Nurul Haque Nur said expatriates harmed by the Middle East crisis will be helped with rehabilitation if they return, and that embassies have been asked to extend the visas of those who cannot travel.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Nurul Haque Nur

facts.statement: State Minister Nurul Haque Nur said the government's aim is to create new labour markets, giving priority to building skilled workers; work is under way on Japan and Europe and talks are going on with several other Asian countries.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Nurul Haque Nur

facts.statement: The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February 2026 and the war spread to 14 Middle Eastern countries. CAAB (Bebichok) says 391 flights were cancelled from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka between 28 February and 11 March 2026, including 24 on Wednesday (11 March).
As of the article (14 March 2026) Iran, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar and Jordan had kept their airspace closed.

Flights to Jeddah and Riyadh in Saudi Arabia remained in operation in March 2026 so some workers were still going, but departures to Saudi Arabia had also fallen; some people were afraid to take visas, and those who had not done their medical test were not taking BMET clearance.
facts.source_in_article: Fakhrul Islam, former joint secretary general of BAIRA

facts.statement: Workers who came home on leave from Oman were stuck in Bangladesh in March 2026 because there were no flights, while their companies were phoning and pressing them to return.
facts.source_in_article: stranded workers Mobarak Hossain and Farhad Hossain

facts.statement: OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam says 4.5 to 5 million (45 to 50 lakh) Bangladeshi workers are in the Middle East.

OKUP chairperson Shakirul Islam suggested the government build a database of people who have paid money but cannot travel, so that they get the chance to go later; migration-sector people also said the government could give emergency support to families that borrowed to migrate and now cannot repay.
RMMRU says Russia is now an important new labour market for Bangladesh: 4,663 Bangladeshis went there in 2025, against 993 the year before.

RMMRU says a ring has begun collecting migrants with the lure of good pay and Russian citizenship, and part of this ring works with a dishonest ring in Russia to send Bangladeshi workers to fight in the Russia-Ukraine war.
From 1 January to 3 October 2025, 15,076 Bangladeshi migrants reached Italy's coast by sea, the highest of any nationality arriving in Italy in that year and about double the previous year's figure.

RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui warned that with regular migration halted, irregular migration risk may rise: people trying to reach Italy could fall into the trap of Libya or Russia rings, and no one should fall for any lure at this moment. She said Bangladesh embassies in war-hit countries must be active and send information home daily.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU

facts.statement: Former BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam said people should wait and decide after understanding the situation, and that the Malaysia market must not be reopened through a syndicate.
facts.source_in_article: Fakhrul Islam, former joint secretary general of BAIRA

headline_en: Why the Bangladeshi passport's standing has fallen: who is responsible, the people or the state?
summary_en: A reader-contributed opinion piece by a migration researcher at Bangladesh Agricultural University argues that the weak standing of the Bangladeshi passport stems both from citizens' conduct (irregular sea migration to Europe, overstaying tourist and student visas, unfounded asylum claims, carrying illegal goods) and from state failures (broker-dependent migration, corruption at passport offices and immigration, passive embassies). It cites the Italian ambassador's figure that over 18,000 Bangladeshis reached Italy by boat via Libya in 2025 and sought asylum. It is mostly general commentary with few concrete facts.

facts.statement: Italy's ambassador in Dhaka, Antonio Alessandro, said that in 2025 more than 18,000 Bangladeshis reached Italy by boat via Libya and applied for asylum (reported in Prothom Alo, 14 November 2025).
facts.source_in_article: Italian ambassador Antonio Alessandro, quoted from Prothom Alo 14 November 2025

facts.statement: Italian ambassador Antonio Alessandro said that if a significant number of Bangladeshis go abroad illegally and misuse the asylum application process abroad, it affects the passport index (ranking).

A BBC Bangla online report of 16 November 2025 said the tendency of Bangladeshis to misuse a visa to move from one country to another has increased, reducing credibility, and that open quarrels among political party supporters abroad also damage the country's image; these were given as reasons for Bangladeshis being refused visas.
facts.source_in_article: BBC Bangla report cited by the writer

facts.statement: The writer states that many Bangladeshis go to the Middle East and other countries on tourist visas, do not return on time and stay and work illegally, which breaches visa conditions; because of this misuse many countries have stopped giving tourist visas to Bangladeshi citizens (no countries are named).

The writer states that reviews of asylum applications by Bangladeshis in Europe, Canada and Australia find most to be unfounded, and that reports of EU migration offices show a large share of Bangladeshi asylum seekers' applications are rejected as unfounded (no figures given).
The writer states that many countries have introduced extra documents, interviews or long verification processes for Bangladeshi citizens, so that genuine students and tourists also face suspicion.
The writer says that, according to UN data, Bangladeshis have been among the top ten nationalities of irregular migrants reaching Europe in recent years.
facts.source_in_article: UN data as cited by the writer

facts.statement: The writer notes that many Bangladeshis carry unnecessary or illegal goods when going abroad and especially when returning (gold or currency above the limit, banned items), which leads foreign immigration officers to mark Bangladeshi passengers as risky travellers.

The writer says Bangladesh's migration sector is broker-dependent: many people are cheated in the name of being sent abroad for work, get work visas on forged papers and then fall into trouble abroad; and that some people get passports on forged documents by paying bribes.

The writer recommends compulsory training and orientation on law and culture for people going abroad, strict verification in passport issuance, awareness campaigns on irregular migration at school, college, union and village level, and exemplary punishment of brokers and human traffickers.

headline_en: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul calls for recruiting more skilled workers from Bangladesh to Saudi Arabia
summary_en: A press release reports that expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul met Saudi vice minister Abdullah bin Nasser Abuthnain on the sidelines of the 7th Global Occupational Safety and Health Conference in Riyadh and asked Saudi Arabia to recruit more skilled Bangladeshi workers for Expo 2030 and the 2034 FIFA World Cup. He proposed checks on employers before work visas are issued and online contract signing before arrival, and promised one-month training for women domestic workers before they get a visa. He also asked Jordan's labour minister to recruit more Bangladeshi men in agriculture, tourism and construction.

facts.statement: In a bilateral meeting in Riyadh with Abdullah bin Nasser Abuthnain, vice minister of Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development, Bangladesh's expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul called for more skilled workers to be recruited from Bangladesh, including for the World Expo in 2030, the FIFA World Cup in 2034 and Saudi mega projects.

Adviser Asif Nazrul proposed to Saudi Arabia: verifying the employer's capacity and whether work is actually available before a work visa is issued; signing the employment contract online before the worker arrives in Saudi Arabia; and designing special training courses for women and men workers on Saudi labour law, work, culture and other essential matters. These were proposals, not agreed measures.

Adviser Asif Nazrul invited Saudi authorities to visit Bangladesh's technical training centres (TTC), restated his interest in reserving one or more TTCs only for training Saudi-bound workers if needed, and asked that Bangladeshi TTC instructors be given special technical and language training in Saudi Arabia so they can train Saudi-bound workers better on return.

Adviser Asif Nazrul said the expatriates' welfare ministry is committed to shortening the training period for domestic workers, and assured the Saudi side that women domestic workers will complete a one-month training before getting a Saudi visa and will be sent to Saudi Arabia after a short training within two weeks of getting the visa; the Saudi vice minister welcomed this decision.

Adviser Asif Nazrul expressed interest in implementing the integrated training programme the Saudi ministry has designed for domestic workers of various countries, and stressed training women domestic workers in using the modern household appliances found in Saudi homes and in the Arabic language.

Following a meeting held on 30 January 2025, a working team of officials from the Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development and the Bangladesh embassy was formed to solve specific problems of irregular Bangladeshi workers in Saudi Arabia.

Under a decision of the latest Foreign Office Consultations, a high-powered task force has been formed to solve the problem of illegal (undocumented) workers in Saudi Arabia and remove irregularities in worker recruitment.
Adviser Asif Nazrul thanked Saudi Arabia for hosting more than 3 million (30 lakh) Bangladeshis.

Adviser Asif Nazrul informed the Saudi side about the 15th Joint Commission and 5th Joint Technical Committee meetings to be held in Dhaka on 8-9 October (2025) and invited the Saudi minister to visit Bangladesh.

In a sideline meeting with Jordan's labour minister Khaled Mahmoud Al Bakkar, adviser Asif Nazrul requested that Jordan recruit more Bangladeshi male workers in agriculture, tourism and construction alongside women workers, and ease the visa process for skilled workers.

Adviser Asif Nazrul took part as a panellist in the 7th Global Occupational Safety and Health Conference at Kingdom Tower, Riyadh; the Bangladesh delegation included senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan of the expatriates' welfare ministry and Bangladesh's ambassador to Saudi Arabia Md. Delwar Hossain.

headline_en: A huge ring of Bangladeshis in Dubai for money laundering: what should be done
summary_en: A column by economic analyst Mamun Rashid argues that only a little over half of potential remittance reaches Bangladesh through official channels and the rest goes through hundi. It gives the bank and open-market dollar rates in October 2024, lists the obstacles to formal remittance named by a parliamentary committee, gives Bangladesh Bank monthly and yearly remittance figures, and cites press reports of money-laundering rings of Bangladeshis in Portugal and Dubai. It suggests better airport treatment and cheaper fares for expatriates.

facts.statement: The columnist says Bangladesh's estimated potential remittance is about USD 45-50 billion a year, while remittance through legal channels may be slightly above USD 24 billion a year, i.e. somewhat under 55 percent of the potential comes through official channels.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Mamun Rashid, citing sector people

facts.statement: In October 2024 expatriates were getting BDT 121 per US dollar through the banking channel, while the open-market rate was at most BDT 123.50 per dollar; the columnist says the closeness of the official and hundi rates made expatriates comfortable sending money through banks.

The parliamentary standing committee on the expatriates' welfare ministry listed 10 obstacles to bank-channel remittance: the exchange-rate gap between legal and illegal channels; expatriate workers lacking valid papers; no or too few branches of Bangladeshi commercial banks abroad; no or too few Bangladeshi money exchange houses/points; high fees or service charges and a ceiling on sending; the dominance of hundi dealers; expatriates or their close relatives having no bank account in Bangladesh; obstacles to sending when the amount is not consistent with income; no way to send income from unauthorised business or work legally; and lack of awareness and encouragement.
facts.source_in_article: parliamentary standing committee, as cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank data: remittance through the banking channel in 2024 was USD 2.11 billion in January, 2.16 billion in February, 1.99 billion in March, 2.04 billion in April, 2.25 billion in May, 2.54 billion in June, 1.91 billion in July and 2.22 billion in August, and more than USD 2 billion in the first 28 days of September.

Bank-channel remittance to Bangladesh was USD 23.92 billion in FY2023-24, USD 21.61 billion in FY2022-23, USD 21.03 billion in FY2021-22 and USD 24.77 billion in FY2020-21 (the highest for any fiscal year, during Covid).

The columnist says at least USD 25 billion a year of remittance is siphoned off through hundi and other means, more than half of what expatriates send, but notes there is no official government statement or written account of this figure.

According to press reports cited by the columnist, Bangladesh Bank found late in 2023 that a ring of 2,500 Bangladeshi nationals had set up a money-laundering base in Portugal, had taken Portuguese citizenship to move money safely, and had laundered BDT 14,500 crore there.
facts.source_in_article: press reports of Bangladesh Bank findings, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: According to press reports cited by the columnist, Dubai is now the main route or 'safe haven' for money laundering from Bangladesh: Bangladeshi businesspeople have opened 13,000 firms in Dubai for laundering, with BDT 65,000 crore invested there.
facts.source_in_article: press reports cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist recommends legalising the status of workers currently abroad, action against some commercial banks or their officials who cleverly encourage hundi, new investment products for remitted money, and notes that easy investment in the capital market by expatriates has still not been made possible.

The columnist supports proposals for more facilities or a separate terminal for expatriates at the airport, certificates and special services linked to the amount remitted legally, cheaper air fares and courteous treatment by cabin crew and at immigration; he says India's IndiGo and Vistara airlines have become popular with Bangladeshi expatriates for such reasons even though they transit via Mumbai or Delhi.

headline_en: Aminul and Ruhul Amin in 'laundering' money to Malaysia
summary_en: A Prothom Alo investigation describes how a syndicate of 100 recruiting agencies controlled sending workers to Malaysia and how an extra 'syndicate fee' of about BDT 107,000 per worker was collected in cash at the Catharsis International office in Dhaka and sent illegally to Bestinet in Malaysia, plus about BDT 150,000 per worker for bought visas. Two syndicate agency owners name Bestinet's Aminul Islam bin Amin Noor as the leader and Mohammad Ruhul Amin alias Swapan of Catharsis as his Bangladesh representative; Ruhul Amin denied it in June 2024. The total laundered is estimated at about BDT 8,750 crore; the ACC has started investigating.

facts.statement: Sending of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia stopped most recently in May 2024; the Malaysian market has closed to Bangladesh repeatedly over allegations of sending workers through a syndicate, bribery and money laundering.

Sending workers from Bangladesh to Malaysia was not open to all recruiting agencies: out of more than 1,500 agencies, a syndicate (chokro) of 100 agencies was formed. Ordinary agency owners say that for every other source country sending workers to Malaysia is open to all agencies.
The government-fixed cost for a Bangladeshi worker to go to Malaysia was BDT 79,000 per person.
facts.source_in_article: survey by Verite Incorporated and four other organisations, May 2023, as cited by reporter

facts.statement: A May 2023 survey by US-based Verite Incorporated and four other organisations found syndicate members charged workers going to Malaysia an average of BDT 544,000 instead of the government-fixed BDT 79,000.
facts.source_in_article: survey by Verite Incorporated and four other organisations (May 2023)

facts.statement: To send a worker to Malaysia the worker's name had to be registered in software called Migram, officially the Foreign Workers Central Management System (FWCMS), owned by Bestinet, the company of Bangladeshi-origin Malaysian citizen Aminul Islam bin Amin Noor. Only syndicate member agencies appeared in the software.
The FWCMS/Migram registration fee is 100 Malaysian ringgit (about BDT 2,700) per worker, paid by the agency through an e-wallet.

Instead of the 100-ringgit registration fee, about BDT 107,000 per worker was taken from syndicate agencies: the local collecting firm kept BDT 7,000 and sent BDT 100,000 illegally to Bestinet in Malaysia. Two agency owners said Bestinet only allowed the 100-ringgit fee to be paid from the e-wallet after BDT 107,000 per worker was deposited; otherwise it was not allowed.
facts.source_in_article: two recruiting agency owners who were in the syndicate

facts.statement: The extra money was deposited in cash at the Madani Avenue, Dhaka office of Catharsis International, the agency owned by Ruhul Amin; its staff received crores of taka in cash every day. Aminul Islam bin Amin Noor took the extra money saying it was for bribes at various levels in Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: two members of the Malaysia syndicate; S M Rafiq of United Export Limited

facts.statement: Fakhrul Islam, managing director of Human Resource Development Centre (an agency outside the syndicate that sent workers through another agency) and BAIRA joint secretary general, said the syndicate agency took a 'syndicate fee' of BDT 152,000 per worker just for arranging the BMET clearance, which actually costs BDT 6,000; air ticket and all other costs had to be paid separately. (This BDT 152,000 differs from the BDT 107,000 per worker cited by syndicate members.)
facts.source_in_article: Fakhrul Islam, BAIRA joint secretary general

facts.statement: Getting BMET clearance for a worker actually costs BDT 6,000, according to BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam.
facts.source_in_article: Fakhrul Islam, BAIRA joint secretary general

facts.statement: In a little over one and a half years, BMET clearance was taken for 492,416 workers in the names of the 100 syndicate agencies.

It is alleged that at least half of the job offers (demand letters) for the 492,416 workers were bought for money, at an average of 6,000 ringgit or BDT 150,000 per worker, known as 'visa trade'; BDT 3,750 crore was laundered this way.
The article estimates about BDT 5,000 crore was laundered to Malaysia as 'syndicate fee' at BDT 100,000 per worker and another BDT 3,750 crore through visa trade, at least BDT 8,750 crore in total.
Bangladesh Bank data: remittance from Malaysia in FY2023-24 was USD 1.12 billion (about BDT 11,000 crore).

Although 12 visa centres were approved for workers' e-visas, only the Malaysia Employment Facilitation Centre (MEFC), the Dhaka office of FWCMS, issued e-visas. MEFC's office was in Catharsis Tower, Banani, Dhaka: Malaysia-bound workers' passports were submitted there for visas and agencies collected them from there.
facts.source_in_article: ministry letter of 2 January 2023; related sources

facts.statement: After a BAIRA complaint, the expatriates' welfare ministry wrote to the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia on 2 January 2023 saying most agencies selected through FWCMS lacked the facilities and capacity to recruit and send workers, that automatic selection of agents created scope to charge high migration costs, and asking that e-visas be issued from more than one centre.

On 9 May 2023 the expatriates' welfare ministry wrote to the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia asking it to take up with the Malaysian government complaints from agencies that Bestinet was not allocating e-wallet top-ups; several Malaysian employer companies had also complained to Malaysia's home ministry.

RJSC records show Malaysia's Bestinet registered in Bangladesh on 24 March 2014 and opened Bestinet Bangladesh Limited, with Aminul Islam bin Amin Noor as chairman and Mohammad Ruhul Amin as managing director; of 12,000 shares, 10,000 were Aminul's and 2,000 Ruhul's. On 28 March 2019 Aminul's shares were transferred to Ruhul and Ruhul's brother Saiful Islam joined as director; in 2022 the company was renamed Catharsis Solutions Limited.
facts.source_in_article: RJSC records found by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Ruhul Amin told Prothom Alo on 20 June 2024 that the allegations of taking and laundering money were false, that both governments gave all approvals and agencies with good contacts in Malaysia got approval after lobbying, and that Bestinet Malaysia has no relation to Bestinet Bangladesh. He could not be reached later and is believed to have left Bangladesh after 5 August 2024.

S M Rafiq, managing director of syndicate member agency United Export Limited, wrote to the Prime Minister's Office on 28 May 2024 alleging that Ruhul Amin alias Swapan and his Malaysian partner Aminul Islam bin Amin Noor were the masterminds of laundering money to Malaysia; he said every syndicate agency had to deliver BDT 107,000 per worker to the Catharsis office.
facts.source_in_article: S M Rafiq, United Export Limited

facts.statement: After 5 August 2024 several BAIRA members filed written complaints with the interim government and the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). A 22 August 2024 letter to the Chief Adviser from BAIRA member Mostafa Mahmud alleged the same pair also built a Malaysia syndicate in 2017 and that the syndicate looted BDT 17,544 crore over the two rounds.
facts.source_in_article: letter of BAIRA member Mostafa Mahmud

facts.statement: The ACC has started investigating allegations against many in the Malaysia syndicate, including four former MPs whose personal and family firms were reported (Prothom Alo, 30 May 2024) to have earned heavily in the syndicate: former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal, Benazir Ahmed, Nizam Uddin Hazari and Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury. The Awami League government took no action against the syndicate.

TIB executive director Iftekharuzzaman said workers from neighbouring countries go to Malaysia at the employer's expense while the rule is different for Bangladesh, and that a ring in Malaysia representing the Bangladeshi syndicate holds workers and the state hostage for illegal business and money laundering.

headline_en: 63 percent of Bangladeshis heading to Europe via Libya end up held captive
summary_en: A BRAC study of 557 Bangladeshis who returned from Libya, released on 23 February 2024, found 63 percent had been held captive after being lured with promises of Europe and good jobs, and most were physically tortured and ransomed. The article gives the study's figures on food, movement, routes, ages, home districts and funding, plus Frontex and UNHCR figures on the Central Mediterranean route. It also reports a 15 February 2024 boat sinking that killed 9 Bangladeshis and the return of 144 Bangladeshis from Libya on 22 February 2024.

facts.statement: A BRAC study analysing 50 types of information on each of 557 Bangladeshis returned from Libya found that 63 percent of those taken to Libya with the lure of being sent to Europe had been held captive, and most had been physically tortured.

BRAC study of 557 Libya returnees: after reaching Libya 68 percent lost freedom of movement; 54 percent said they never got three meals a day; at least 22 percent got only one meal a day; of those held captive, 93 percent were held in camps and 79 percent were physically tortured.

BRAC says everyone taken to Libya with the lure of Europe is promised a good job but does not get one; most are held in camps in Libya, tortured, and held hostage while money is extorted from their families.
BRAC study of 557 Libya returnees: the families of 60 percent had been lured by local brokers with the promise of a good job, but 89 percent got no job or work of any kind.

BRAC study of 557 Libya returnees: the most-used route was Dhaka to Dubai to Egypt to Libya; others went Dhaka-Istanbul-Dubai-Libya, Dhaka-Qatar-Libya, Dhaka-Dubai-Syria-Libya, and a few went from Dhaka directly to Libya.

BRAC study: people aged 26 to 40 most often attempt to enter Europe via Libya, with ages 31 to 35 the largest group; most are from Madaripur, Shariatpur, Faridpur, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Munshiganj, Noakhali, Brahmanbaria and Cumilla districts.
BRAC study: asked where they got the money to go to Europe via Libya, 56 percent of returnees said they raised it themselves and 23 percent said they took financial help from family.

Frontex data: Bangladeshis heading for Europe most often choose the sea crossing from Libya, known as the Central Mediterranean route; at least 70,906 Bangladeshis entered Europe by this route from 2009 to 2023.

UNHCR data as cited: since 2015 (the article says 'to June this year') 2.5 million people of various countries crossed the sea to Europe this way and about 22,000 drowned, many Bangladeshis among them. BRAC says Bangladesh has been in the top ten nationalities crossing the Mediterranean irregularly to Europe for a decade.
On 15 February 2024 a boat going from Libya towards Europe sank and 9 Bangladeshis died; 26 Bangladeshis were rescued injured.
On Thursday 22 February 2024, 144 Bangladeshis returned home from Libya.

BRAC associate director Shariful Hasan (Migration and Youth Platform) said ordinary people and aspiring migrants must become aware first, law enforcement must identify local brokers and trafficking rings and run coordinated drives, especially tracing the money transactions, and action is needed against international trafficking rings in Libya and elsewhere.

headline_en: Overseas labour market limited to a few countries
summary_en: An analysis of BMET data for 2019-2023 shows that although 168 countries are on the government's overseas employment list, 97 percent of workers went to only 10 countries and about 55 percent went to Saudi Arabia. The article notes market closures and reopenings (UAE, Oman, Maldives, Malaysia), the difficulty of applying for European visas via India, and Romania's withdrawal of its Dhaka consular service after one month in 2023. Experts warn of the risk of depending on a few countries.

facts.statement: Analysis of BMET data for 2019-2023: 168 countries are on the government's overseas employment list, but 97 percent of all workers sent abroad went to just 10 countries; workers went to 137 countries in total over the five years (counting any country with at least one worker), and 31 listed countries received no worker.
facts.source_in_article: BMET data analysed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Every worker going abroad legally for work must take clearance (chharpotro) from the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), which keeps the records of workers sent.

Bangladesh began sending workers abroad in 1976 and has sent more than 16 million (1 crore 60 lakh) in 48 years; Saudi Arabia accounts for 35 percent of the total, and about 55 percent of workers who left in the latest five years (2019-2023) went to Saudi Arabia.

In 2019-2023 only eight countries received more than 10,000 Bangladeshi workers a year on average, taking over 95 percent of workers: Saudi Arabia, Oman, Malaysia, United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Qatar, Kuwait and Jordan. Seventeen countries received more than 5,000 a year on average; 91 countries received fewer than 100 a year on average.
facts.source_in_article: BMET data analysed by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: BMET data: the highest overseas employment in Bangladesh's history was in 2022 and 2023, with more than 100,000 workers leaving per month on average. Even so, six countries received one worker each in 2023 after none in the four previous years, and 16 countries received only 35 workers in five years.

Migration experts say expatriate workers themselves open the way for new workers: they collect labour demand abroad and send it for acquaintances and relatives at home; about 90 percent of demand letters reach Bangladesh this way.
The UAE labour market was closed to Bangladeshis for four years in a row; in the last two years (2022-2023) the number of workers going there rose.
Towards the end of 2023 Oman announced it was stopping visas for Bangladeshis.

The Maldives labour market was closed to Bangladeshis because of the large number of undocumented workers, and no new workers could be sent for four years; sending workers to the Maldives started again from 2024.
Workers had been going to Malaysia for two years as of February 2024, with more than 350,000 going in 2023 alone; before that the Malaysian market was closed for three years in a row.

Legal sending of workers to Italy increased in 2022 and 2023, bringing Italy into the top ten destinations for 2019-2023 with more than 25,000 workers; most Bangladeshis in Italy went by irregular means, and many still cross the Mediterranean and die in accidents. Departures to Romania also rose over the two years.

Workers go to South Korea mainly under government management; demand rises every year, but private recruiting agencies cannot send workers because they do not get clearance. Sri Lanka, Nepal, Vietnam, China, the Philippines and India send workers to Korea.

BAIRA secretary general Ali Haider Chowdhury said that for several European countries there is no embassy in Dhaka, so applicants must go to India to apply for a visa, a complicated process that harms Bangladesh; he urged the government to arrange embassy or consular services in Dhaka through diplomatic agreement.
facts.source_in_article: Ali Haider Chowdhury, secretary general of BAIRA

facts.statement: RMMRU says Romania opened a consular service in Dhaka in February 2023 but withdrew it from Bangladesh within a month under pressure from influential quarters to give visas to their own people first, although Romania had planned to take 15,000 workers in 6 months.

BMET carried out a study in 2018 on the potential for sending workers to 53 countries; over a decade and a half the government expanded the list from 97 to 168 countries, but in most of them only a handful of workers go.

Additional secretary (planning and development) Md. Alamgir Hossain of the expatriates' welfare ministry said the research wing works regularly to find new markets, and that the emphasis is on sending skilled workers rather than more workers.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Alamgir Hossain, additional secretary, expatriates' welfare ministry

facts.statement: RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui said the claim of sending workers to 168 countries is not reasonable; the market is limited to 10-11 countries, dependence on them is a big risk, and there is a lack of coordination between the ministry's plans and its work.

headline_en: Start of worker recruitment for Malaysia announced; how workers will be recruited
summary_en: On Thursday 15 October 2026 the expatriates' welfare ministry announced by press release that the recruitment process for workers going to Malaysia has begun, through listed and approved recruiting agencies and approved medical centres. Malaysia has listed government-owned BOESL and 25 private agencies as processing/service agencies and allowed another 312 agencies to work; the release sets out four steps from demand letter to BMET clearance. Malaysia has agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers entirely free of cost, and medical tests will start at the centres currently listed on the Malaysian website.

facts.statement: On 15 October 2026 Bangladesh's Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment announced in a press release the start of the recruitment process for people wishing to go to Malaysia as workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment press release

facts.statement: Workers interested in Malaysia can complete the process through a listed and approved recruiting agency and must do their health test at an approved medical centre, according to the ministry's 15 October 2026 release.

Under the memorandum of understanding signed between Bangladesh and Malaysia on 18 December 2022, selecting and listing recruiting agencies is the responsibility of Malaysia's Ministry of Human Resources; the ministry says Malaysia applies its own policies and eligibility conditions to its other source countries too.

During the interim government, vetting of recruiting agencies against Malaysia's conditions began; Malaysia relaxed some conditions during talks, and a list of 423 recruiting agencies was then sent to the Malaysian authorities.

Malaysian authorities listed Bangladesh's only state recruiting agency, Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), and 25 private agencies as 'processing agencies' or 'service agencies', and gave a further 312 recruiting agencies the opportunity to work.
A listed agency may find employers on its own initiative, collect its own demand letters, select its own workers in Bangladesh and carry out their recruitment according to the rules.
The expatriates' welfare ministry says that at the Bangladesh government's special request the Malaysian authorities have agreed in principle to take 10,000 workers entirely free of cost.

Malaysia recruitment step 1: every valid and eligible recruiting agency approved by the Malaysian authorities collects demand letters from the Malaysian labour market on its own initiative. Step 2: the agency that collected the demand letter selects and recruits its own workers following Bangladesh's laws and rules.

Malaysia recruitment step 3: where administrative processing with Malaysian authorities is needed (calling visa, e-visa or other set official procedures), BOESL and the other 25 listed processing agencies provide the necessary support.

Malaysia recruitment step 4: the recruiting agency takes clearance from BMET; any listed agency can do this, i.e. the clearance can be issued in the name of the agency in whose name the demand letter came. BOESL and the 25 other processing agencies can give the approved agency a no-objection letter for the BMET clearance.

The ministry says a worker must not be made to bear an extra financial burden for Malaysian employment and the government wants the process to be as affordable, safe and transparent as possible; the release states no cost figure.

Finalising approved medical centres for Malaysia-bound workers is ongoing and is a joint responsibility of Bangladesh and Malaysia under the MoU. Bangladesh asked for the existing medical centres to be changed; a joint delegation of Malaysia's health, human resources and home ministries will come to Bangladesh, inspect every centre and then give final approval.

For now it has been decided to start with the medical centres currently listed on the relevant Malaysian website; if irregularities are found Bangladeshi authorities will force the centre to stop operating, and any newly added centres will be published on that website (the release does not name the website).
The release says the Prime Minister made reopening and expanding labour markets a priority, gave Malaysia special importance and made his first foreign trip to Malaysia.

headline_en: Expatriates' welfare minister hears expatriates' expectations in Los Angeles
summary_en: At a California BNP anniversary picnic in Griffith Park, Los Angeles on 30 August 2026, expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury held an hour-long exchange with expatriates. He spoke of plans to finalise a 'Probashi Card', put the whole worker-sending process online, run a month-long awareness campaign against irregular migration, and support families of those who die abroad and returnees. Expatriates asked for less harassment in investing, quick service and lounges at the airport, and transparency of recruiting agencies.

facts.statement: Expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said that introducing a 'Probashi Card' (expatriate card) will be finalised as part of the government's 180-day programme; the article gives no details of what the card offers.

Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said an initiative is being taken to make the entire process of sending workers abroad online, bringing more transparency to recruiting agencies' legality, overseas labour demand and related information management.

Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said efforts are under way to identify and act against rings that send people abroad illegally, and that a wide awareness campaign will be run in several districts over the following month to reduce migration by sea or illegal routes.

Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury gave an assurance that when a Bangladeshi dies abroad, besides bringing the body home, the family will get financial help and the children help with their education (no amounts stated).
Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury described a government plan to reintegrate returnee workers with financial and logistic support according to their previous occupation.

Expatriates in Los Angeles demanded less bureaucratic complexity and harassment when investing in Bangladesh, a 'quick service' at the airport and a comfortable VIP lounge during flight delays, better Hajj camp facilities, and transparency and accountability of recruiting agencies including on the Malaysia 'syndicate' issue.
The minister asked expatriates in Los Angeles to tell him of any problem by email or phone (no address or number printed), saying the issues would be recorded and acted on.

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis' work permits cancelled in Singapore for extremist posts on social media
summary_en: Singapore's Internal Security Department (ISD) told The Straits Times on 17 July 2026 that two Bangladeshi construction workers, Rishad Tayani (25) and Shahedul Islam (37), had their work permits cancelled in July after investigations into extremist social media posts, and were sent back to Bangladesh. They were detained on arrival at Dhaka airport on 8 July and remanded by a Dhaka court on 9 July. The article recalls earlier cases of Bangladeshi workers arrested or repatriated from Singapore for extremism in 2015, 2016 and 2020.

facts.statement: In July 2026 Singapore cancelled the work permits of two Bangladeshi construction workers, Rishad Tayani (25) and Shahedul Islam (37), after separate Internal Security Department (ISD) investigations into social media posts supporting extremism, and sent them back to Bangladesh.
facts.source_in_article: ISD, to The Straits Times, 17 July 2026

facts.statement: ISD said Rishad Tayani's post expressed support for Bangladeshi radical Islamist writer Shafiur Rahman Farabi, and Shahedul Islam posted inflammatory content on the Israel-Iran conflict and sectarian statements such as calling Muslims who oppose Islamic law 'kafir'.

ISD said its investigation found no evidence that the two men planned any attack in Singapore or were involved in terrorist activity, but their extremist and divisive views were harmful to Singapore's multiracial, multi-religious society; their work permits were cancelled on that basis.

According to Bangladeshi media, the two workers returned from Singapore were detained on arrival at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka on 8 July 2026, and three phones and three passports were seized; on 9 July they were taken to a Dhaka court, where police sought and the judge granted remand.

In the remand application Dhaka police said the two men admitted being involved with a militant group while in Singapore and needed further questioning about contacts, network and funding sources. Rishad told the court he was arrested in Singapore for writing on Facebook in 2023 about a man named Farabi.
facts.source_in_article: police remand application; Rishad in court

facts.statement: In 2020 a Bangladeshi construction worker who had worked in Singapore since 2017 was arrested there; the investigation found he had become radicalised after viewing pro-IS material online, was planning an armed attack and had bought folding knives to use in an attack back home.

In 2016 ISD detained eight Bangladeshis working in Singapore's construction and marine sectors who were members of a secret group called 'Islamic State in Bangladesh', had documents on weapons and bomb-making, planned to recruit other Bangladeshi workers and raised funds to buy arms for attacks in Bangladesh. Five more Bangladeshi workers, not in the group but found with jihadi books, were also sent home.
In 2015, 27 Bangladeshis working in Singapore's construction sector were arrested for forming a jihadi terrorist group and considering armed jihad abroad; they were later sent back to Bangladesh.

headline_en: Where does the cheating of remittance fighters end? What is the role of the embassies?
summary_en: An opinion column by a Canada-based analyst argues that state bodies for migrant workers (BMET, BOESL, DEMO offices, TTCs, Wage Earners' Welfare Board, Probashi Kallyan Bank) do not reach villages, so aspiring migrants turn to brokers who overcharge. It cites CPD, World Bank and ITUC findings, including that only 15,294 of over 1.1 million workers in 2023 went through BOESL and that average migration cost approaches BDT 400,000. It proposes seven measures, including labour market cells in embassies and upazila-level one-stop support centres.

facts.statement: The columnist states that expatriates sent more than USD 30 billion in remittance to Bangladesh in FY2024-25; later in the same column he says expatriate workers are sending more than USD 35 billion a year (the two figures are given separately).

The columnist lists the state institutions meant to support migrant workers: BMET, BOESL, DEMO offices, technical training centres, the Wage Earners' Welfare Board and Probashi Kallyan Bank; on the digital side, the OEP-BMET platform and the Ami Probashi app.
A 2024 CPD study found that while more than 1.1 million workers went abroad in 2023, only 15,294 went through the state recruiting agency BOESL, just 1.3 percent of the total.
facts.source_in_article: CPD study (2024), cited by the columnist

facts.statement: A World Bank assessment says BMET's several databases are not linked to each other, so a full labour market information system has not been built; DEMO offices' capacity is also not enough to reach the large population in remote areas.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank assessment, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: By the World Bank's estimate the average cost of going abroad for Bangladeshi workers reaches close to BDT 400,000 (about four lakh taka), a large part of which goes to middlemen.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: An ITUC survey says recruitment in rural areas is often done verbally, with no receipt and no proof, so legal remedy becomes hard if the worker is cheated. The columnist says brokers exploit acquaintance and trust: sometimes taking extra money, sometimes giving false promises, sometimes trapping people in debt.

The columnist proposes (as recommendations, not existing measures): a Labour Market Development Cell (LMDC) in every embassy and high commission to find new jobs; one-stop support for foreign employers so selected workers can leave within four to six weeks; performance-based incentives for embassy officials; a 'safe overseas employment support centre' in every upazila uniting BMET, DEMO, BOESL, TTC and Probashi Kallyan Bank with mobile camps at union level.

The columnist also proposes: publishing verified job information in simple Bangla (country, job, salary, government fee, agency fee, training and medical costs) on office boards and online; registering local facilitators under BMET with fixed fees and compulsory receipts; translating every job contract into Bangla with a verification certificate; expanding BOESL to districts and upazilas; and making Probashi Kallyan Bank's low-interest loans available directly without brokers.

headline_en: Opening the Malaysian labour market is not enough; the whole migration system must change
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Selim Reza of North South University, written before Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's upcoming visit to Malaysia in June 2026, argues that the visit should be used to build a syndicate-free, transparent, digital recruitment framework rather than just reopen the market, which had been stalled for two years. It recounts the open-close history of the Malaysian market (2008, 2016, 2018, 2022, 2024), calls for a regularisation programme for undocumented Bangladeshis, regional consular services, and a shift to skilled workers. It is commentary with few hard facts.

facts.statement: The columnist recounts the history of the Malaysian labour market for Bangladeshis: worker sending began in 1978 with a few workers; the market closed in 2008, reopened in 2016, closed again in 2018, reopened in a new form in 2022 and was suspended again in 2024.

As of mid-June 2026 the Malaysian labour market had been stalled for two years, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's upcoming visit to Malaysia raised expectations of reopening the market and of legalisation of undocumented Bangladeshis (these were expectations, not announced outcomes).

The columnist says Malaysia suspended the market several times because of opaque recruitment, the monopoly influence of a limited number of agencies, extra money taken from workers, breach of contract, human trafficking allegations and administrative weakness.

The columnist says that after past openings a few influential recruiting agencies or groups took control of the whole recruitment process, leading to extra charges, false job promises and contract violations; many workers sold land, borrowed at high interest or mortgaged family assets, and their earnings in the first two to three years abroad went mainly to repaying debt.

The columnist says most undocumented Bangladeshis in Malaysia are not involved in crime but lost legal status through employer fraud, company closure, visa renewal complications or administrative weakness.

The columnist recommends that Bangladesh negotiate with Malaysia a special regularisation programme letting undocumented workers return to legal status by paying a fine or meeting set conditions, and more flexible procedures for changing workplace, changing employer and renewing visas (a recommendation, not an existing programme).

Bangladeshis working across Malaysia's states must travel to Kuala Lumpur for most consular services; coming from Sabah, Sarawak, Penang or Johor to Kuala Lumpur to renew a passport or get other services is time-consuming and costly. The columnist calls for regional consular service centres, mobile consular services and full digital services.

The columnist says most Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia are low-skilled or unskilled, in construction, agriculture, cleaning or general manufacturing with comparatively low pay, while Malaysia is investing in semiconductors, electric vehicles, renewable energy, data centres, smart manufacturing and robotics; he expects demand for electrical and mechanical technicians, automation operators, advanced welders, solar technicians, semiconductor technicians, IT and network support staff, smart-agriculture technicians and healthcare assistants to grow over the next decade.

The columnist recommends a digital, transparent recruitment framework with Malaysia in which worker selection, job contract, employer information, visa process and cost details are open and verifiable online, each worker's recruitment cost is made public, and no monopoly recruitment arrangement is accepted; he also suggests a joint Bangladesh-Malaysia skills development programme and joint training centres in Bangladesh.

headline_en: He might not survive, so he recited the kalema before sleeping at night
summary_en: At an RMMRU press conference at the National Press Club on Wednesday 13 May 2026 on the Iran and Gulf war's effect on Bangladeshi migrants, RMMRU said about 5 million Bangladeshis are in the Gulf and Middle East, at least 9 workers have died, 200 workers were evacuated from Iran, and March 2026 employment clearances were down 50 percent year on year. Three returnees from Iran, all from Cumilla, described fleeing with debts and asked for rehabilitation support. RMMRU reported layoffs and wage cuts in the Gulf and recommended 24-hour Bangla hotlines, an emergency return guideline, an emergency fund and a monitoring dashboard.

facts.statement: RMMRU says 82 percent of Bangladeshi workers who went abroad in 2025 went to the Middle East and Gulf countries, and 46 percent of remittance came from these countries.
RMMRU's written statement says about 5 million (50 lakh) Bangladeshi expatriates are in the Gulf region and Middle East.
RMMRU says at least 9 Bangladeshi workers had died because of the Iran/Gulf war as of 13 May 2026; no Bangladeshi was killed or injured in Iran itself.
RMMRU says employment clearances to go abroad in March 2026 were down 50 percent compared with March of the previous year.

After the war began, Bangladeshis in Iran who contacted the Bangladesh embassy asking to return were evacuated and brought home through the International Organization for Migration (IOM): because flights from Iran were suspended they were taken by road to Azerbaijan and flown home. 186 people returned on 21 March 2026 and 14 more on 11 April 2026 (200 in total).
Workers in Iran who wanted to leave during the war contacted the Bangladesh embassy, which arranged their rescue and return through IOM via Azerbaijan.

RMMRU reports that a packaging worker at the warehouse of an app-based delivery company in Saudi Arabia said the warehouse had more than 400 workers and now has only 65; the rest were all laid off because sales fell.
facts.source_in_article: a warehouse packaging worker in Saudi Arabia, via RMMRU

facts.statement: RMMRU says workers in the Gulf region are suffering widespread wage cuts, those without a fixed job have no income, and living costs and air fares have risen.
RMMRU says southern Lebanon is under continuous Israeli attack and Bangladeshi women domestic workers working in Lebanon face extreme risk.
RMMRU says the lives and livelihoods of 2 million (20 lakh) Bangladeshis living in the United Arab Emirates could be put at risk by the war.

RMMRU says Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 mega projects were expected to create jobs, but if they are disrupted by falling investor confidence, rising costs or direct infrastructure damage, job opportunities will shrink.

RMMRU notes that when civil war began in Libya in 2011 about 40,000 Bangladeshi migrant workers were repatriated; it says significant gaps remain in capacity for large-scale repatriation, communication and legal protection.

RMMRU recommends: 24-hour Bangla-language hotlines in countries involved in the war; a guideline with emergency return rules and necessary information sent to embassies; an emergency fund from the revenue budget; and a monitoring dashboard showing cancelled flights, stranded migrants, visa status and return information.

RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui said returnees need rehabilitation as during the Covid pandemic, those stranded in the war need regular support, irregular migration may rise as jobs fall, and the government could form an inter-ministerial committee including civil society.

headline_en: Services for workers going abroad must be brought under one umbrella
summary_en: At a roundtable on 'Rights of women migrant workers and safe migration' held on Tuesday 5 May 2026 at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, organised by Badabon Sangho and Prothom Alo, speakers said women migrants lack skills and still face syndicates, excess costs, bribes, brokers and institutional corruption. State Minister Nurul Haque described plans for district one-stop services, a Probashi Card, a standard migration cost, agency grading, legal firms abroad and a rehabilitation fund. Officials, UN agencies and NGOs made further calls; almost all items are plans or demands rather than measures in force.

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Nurul Haque described plans (not yet in force) to bring district manpower offices, Probashi Kallyan Bank and welfare centres into the same building as a one-stop service for women wishing to go abroad, to introduce a 'Probashi Card' for expatriates, to set a standard migration cost, and to introduce a grading system to identify good recruiting agencies.

State Minister Nurul Haque spoke of plans to send women workers abroad after skilling them, to appoint legal firms abroad for their protection, to ensure digital banking facilities, and to create a large special fund for rehabilitating returnees.

State Minister Nurul Haque said the government has noticed that 23 ministries give some similar training, wasting public money without results, and that training by any ministry or body needs to be brought into one process.

A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, director (finance and budget) of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, said the Board stands by people abroad in illness, death or legal complications, and tries to support any expatriate, woman or man, from the time they cross immigration until they return.
facts.source_in_article: A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: ILO senior national programme manager Rahnuma Salam Khan said unclear information is the main cause of exploitation of women workers, called for reform of the technical training centres (TTCs), and described a plan to introduce a special cash scheme for returnee women with ILO support.

Farzana Shahnaz, national programme officer (reintegration, labour mobility and social inclusion), said Union Digital Centre (UDC) entrepreneurs should be trained to deliver correct information and counselling at grassroots level, and that a profit-and-loss calculation should be done before going abroad to reduce migration cost and debt burden.

BOESL deputy manager (overseas recruitment) Nu-Emong Marma said those who go abroad through the state company BOESL stay free of fraud and become self-reliant because BOESL ensures protection of workers' rights at workplaces abroad.

UNDP Bangladesh gender expert Sharmin Islam said women migrants suffer extreme loneliness and mental stress from long separation and hostile conditions, and called for mental health services to be prioritised alongside pay and physical safety and for psychosocial counselling in rehabilitating returnee women.

Other speakers' demands: a five-year master plan and the right to organise (Syed Sultan Uddin Ahmed, BILS); transparency and accountability in recruitment (Marina Sultana, RMMRU); stronger labour wings in Bangladesh embassies and an effective legal framework (Jasiya Khatun, WARBE Development Foundation); bringing local brokers under a legal framework (S K Mojibul Haque, BNSK); more government activity in destination countries and social security for returnee women (Lipi Rahman, Badabon Sangho).

Razekuzzaman Ratan, president of Samajtantrik Sramik Front, said the pattern of the Middle East market will change after the war and Bangladesh must prepare accordingly; he said women go abroad with great promise and return to neglect.

headline_en: War is obstructing sending workers to several Middle East labour markets: minister in parliament
summary_en: Answering questions tabled in parliament on Sunday 5 April 2026, expatriates' welfare minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the ongoing Iran war with the US and Israel is obstructing the sending of workers to several Middle East markets including the UAE. He gave 2025 overseas employment figures, said the government does not want to send workers to Malaysia through a syndicate of a few agencies, and said the agreement with Saudi Arabia ensures women domestic workers can keep a mobile phone.

headline_en: Emphasis on building alternative labour markets
summary_en: Published on International Migrants Day, 18 December 2025, the article reports BMET data showing the share of skilled workers among those going abroad fell from about 26 percent in FY2023-24 to 18 percent in FY2024-25, with 59 percent going as low-skilled. It lists the interim government's steps towards skilled markets: a Japan Cell with a target of 100,000 workers in five years, MoUs with a South Korean province and with Italy, removal of attestation for Singapore, language courses at 44 TTCs and skill testing at 15 TTCs under a deal with Saudi firm Takamol. RMMRU says TTC certificates are not internationally recognised.

facts.statement: BMET data: 1,198,900 workers went abroad in FY2023-24, about 26 percent of them skilled; 1,015,312 went in FY2024-25, of whom 18 percent were skilled, only 3 percent professional, skilled and semi-skilled together 38 percent, and the remaining 59 percent low-skilled.
Every worker sent abroad must take clearance from the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET).

BMET data: Bangladesh lists 168 destination countries, but from January to 15 December 2025 workers went to 141 countries, 1,066,759 in total; 13 countries got one worker each, only 8 countries got more than 10,000, and two got more than 100,000: Qatar with 100,000 (one lakh) and Saudi Arabia with more than 700,000.
The expatriates' welfare ministry formed a 'Japan Cell' and adopted a special language and skills training project with the target of sending 100,000 skilled workers to Japan in five years.

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul said more than 6,000 workers were sent to Japan in just six months, over 50 percent more than the previous year.
A memorandum of understanding was signed with a province of South Korea to send seasonal workers, and sending has begun.

facts.statement: Japanese, English, Chinese and Korean language courses are being run at 44 technical training centres (TTCs); caregiver training, previously unavailable at TTCs, has been added because of rising demand abroad.
Under an agreement signed between BMET and the Saudi company Takamol, 15 TTCs gained the capacity to conduct skill tests in the past year.

Adviser Asif Nazrul said an international nursing certification preparation course has been launched and work has begun to send skilled nurses to Europe; he expects notable success in sending skilled workers within three years if programmes continue.

At the expatriates' welfare ministry's event at Osmani Auditorium on 17 December 2025, cheques were distributed for migrant workers' insurance benefits, medical and financial assistance, compensation and education stipends for expatriates' children; CIPs among expatriates and banks bringing most remittance were honoured.
Sector people say a worker can earn three to four times more in Japan or European countries than the average monthly pay a worker gets in the Middle East.

Recruiting agencies, NGOs and officials say worker recruitment runs mainly through brokers or acquaintances; workers mainly go into construction and infrastructure, where no skill is needed and pay is low.

headline_en: Bangladesh tops Malaysia's labour market; there is fear and unease too
summary_en: A report from Malaysia says Bangladeshis are now the largest group of foreign workers there (37 percent; 803,332 with work permits at end-June 2025) but many are undocumented and are regularly caught in immigration raids and sent home, which unsettles legal residents too. It gives Malaysia's minimum wage and working hours, yearly worker departures and remittance from Malaysia, the terms of the Malaysia My Second Home programme, and stories of workers who paid BDT 500,000 through brokers. RMMRU's Tasneem Siddiqui urges legalising undocumented Bangladeshis rather than handing the market to a syndicate again.

facts.statement: According to Malaysian media, 182 Bangladeshis were detained in Malaysia in November 2025 alone, and 377 were caught in one raid in September 2025; Bangladeshis are detained in almost every Malaysian immigration department raid and those detained are later sent back to Bangladesh.

A report in Malaysian outlet The Star says Bangladeshis are now the largest group of foreign workers in Malaysia at 37 percent, and 803,332 Bangladeshis held work permits at the end of June 2025. Bangladeshis living there say the real number working is about double that.

An IOM report says that up to 2024, 2.5 million people who entered Malaysia as visitors did not return to their own countries, 38 percent of them Bangladeshi; Bangladeshis in Malaysia say many also went on education (student) visas and did not return.
Malaysia's minimum wage is 1,700 ringgit a month (about BDT 51,000). Workers work 8 hours a day and 45 hours a week, and may do up to four hours of overtime a day if they wish.

Because Malaysia has a fixed minimum wage, many firms hire undocumented workers to save costs, most of them Bangladeshis. There is demand for workers in construction, factories, palm plantations, electrician work, plumbing, painting and supermarkets.

The first 23 Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia in 1978; a formal manpower recruitment agreement was signed in 1992; the market closed on 31 May 2024 and, the article says, was later reopened under various conditions.
Bangladeshi workers going to Malaysia: 50,090 in 2022; 351,683 in 2023 (the highest ever); 93,632 in 2024 up to the ban; and 2,486 in 2025 up to May.

Remittance to Bangladesh from Malaysia: USD 1.02 billion in FY2021-22, 1.12 billion in FY2022-23, 1.60 billion in FY2023-24 and 2.80 billion in FY2024-25; in FY2025-26, USD 260 million in July and 270 million each in August and September 2025.

A group of Bangladeshi workers from Cumilla met near Sultan Abdul Samad Jamek Mosque, Kuala Lumpur in the last week of November 2025 said each had spent BDT 500,000 through a broker to come and had still not got work; they were trying for jobs in a factory outside the capital.
facts.source_in_article: workers from Cumilla, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Mominul Islam of Chuadanga, a shop worker at Times Square, Kuala Lumpur, borrowed BDT 500,000 to go to Malaysia and now earns 2,200 ringgit a month (BDT 66,000); he has repaid the loan.

Under the 'Malaysia My Second Home' programme, a 5-year visa is available for an investment of BDT 3.6 crore (3 crore 60 lakh) and a 20-year visa for a larger sum, on condition of investing in real estate; 3,604 Bangladeshis had joined by 2024, the fourth-largest nationality.

RMMRU founding chair Tasneem Siddiqui said that instead of showpiece manpower export, steps should be taken to legalise undocumented Bangladeshis in Malaysia, noting Malaysia has given such legalisation before; if the market is handed to a syndicate again, workers will not actually be able to join work.
facts.source_in_article: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi in a senior post at a Malaysian technology firm, speaking anonymously, said perhaps half the Bangladeshis seen anywhere there are undocumented, which embarrasses long-settled families and raises questions at their workplaces.
facts.source_in_article: an unnamed Bangladeshi professional in Malaysia
